opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a spectrum. At the simplest end, scientists use models the way they'd use a very knowledgeable colleague down the hall: explaining a technique they haven't used before, summarizing a dense paper outside their subfield, helping draft a methods section, or debugging an analysis script at eleven at night. That's not glamorous, but it removes a lot of friction, and friction adds up in a lab.

One step up, people use models as genuine thinking partners. You describe an unexpected result, say a band on a gel that shouldn't be there or a phenotype that doesn't match your hypothesis, and the model helps you brainstorm explanations and the controls that would distinguish them. What's interesting is that the value isn't always that the model is right. It's that it surfaces possibilities you hadn't considered, and you as the expert can quickly decide which ones are worth chasing.

Then there's a more sophisticated tier where models work across large bodies of knowledge to connect dots: linking a finding in one organism to a pathway studied in another, or spotting that a compound tested for one indication might be relevant to a completely different one. Humans can do this, but no one person can hold the whole literature in their head.

And at the frontier, we're starting to see models take part in the experimental loop itself: proposing protocols, interpreting data as it comes in, and suggesting the next experiment. That's where the most excitement is, and also where you need the most care, because the stakes of being wrong go up and you still need a scientist's judgment.

What I find encouraging is that most people start at the simple end and naturally move up as they build trust and learn what the models are good at. The researchers who get the most out of it treat the model as a collaborator they push on, question, and verify, rather than an oracle.

r001.rationale: The response describes a spectrum of AI use, but it does not contrast optimizing pipetting steps with designing an enzyme.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as a really wide spectrum, and honestly the low end of that spectrum gets undersold.

At the most basic level, a lot of scientists are using these models the way anyone else would: drafting an email to a collaborator, cleaning up a methods section, summarizing a paper they don't have time to read closely. That sounds mundane, but a postdoc's time is one of the scarcest resources in a lab, and if you give them back a few hours a week, that compounds. So I don't dismiss it.

Then there's a middle tier, which is probably where most of the real value is landing right now. That's things like writing analysis scripts, debugging a pipeline that's been broken for two days, converting a protocol from one instrument's format to another, or asking the model to sanity-check an experimental design before you spend expensive reagents on it. The model isn't doing the science, but it's removing friction around the science. A lot of bench scientists aren't trained programmers, and suddenly they can do data analysis they would have previously handed off or just not done.

And then at the high end, you start to see people using models as something closer to a thinking partner or a hypothesis generator. Feeding in a set of results and asking what mechanisms could explain them. Asking the model to pull together literature across fields that the scientist themselves wouldn't normally read. Or in the more automated setups, having the model propose the next experiment, run it through a robotic platform, look at the results, and iterate. That's still early and it's not evenly distributed, but it's where things are heading.

What's interesting to me is that sophistication isn't really about the task, it's about how the scientist treats the output. The people getting the most out of it are skeptical in a productive way. They know the model can be confidently wrong about a protein interaction or a dosage, so they verify, they push back, they ask for the reasoning. The ones who get burned are usually the ones who either trust it blindly or dismiss it entirely after one bad answer. So part of the range you're describing is actually a range in how people have learned to work with the tool, not just what they're using it for.

r001.rationale: The response describes a spectrum of AI uses, but it does not contrast optimizing pipetting steps with designing an enzyme.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a spectrum. At one end, scientists use a model to help with everyday tasks: writing code, understanding a paper, or troubleshooting an analysis. Those uses can be incredibly valuable, even if they’re relatively straightforward.

Then you move toward using the model as a thought partner: asking it to suggest hypotheses, critique an experimental design, or help interpret an unexpected result. That requires more context and much more careful checking, because a plausible explanation isn’t necessarily a correct one.

At the other end, you can imagine models connected to tools and laboratory workflows, helping propose experiments, analyze the results, and inform what to try next. The distinction there is how much responsibility the model has within the research process, and how you validate each step. More sophisticated doesn’t automatically mean more useful. Sometimes helping a scientist get through a coding bottleneck is exactly what moves the science forward.

r001.rationale: The response describes a spectrum from everyday AI assistance to models integrated with lab workflows, but it does not contrast optimizing pipetting steps with designing an enzyme.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty broad spectrum. At one end, scientists use models for everyday tasks: reading papers, writing code, or troubleshooting an analysis. Those tasks may sound straightforward, but they can take up a lot of a scientist’s time.

Then there’s using a model as a thought partner—asking it to critique a hypothesis, suggest an experimental design, or help interpret a surprising result. That requires more context and more judgment from the scientist, because a plausible explanation isn’t necessarily a correct one.

At the more sophisticated end, you can imagine integrating models into a loop with experimental tools: proposing an experiment, looking at the results, and helping decide what to try next. The key distinction is how you check the model’s work. In science, ultimately, your ideas have to survive contact with evidence.

r001.rationale: The response describes a spectrum from everyday tasks to model-guided experimental loops, but does not contrast optimizing pipetting steps with designing an enzyme.
